Summer precipitation emerges as the dominant factor controlling secondary growth with a pronounced latitudinal gradient that is strongest at the southernmost sites and progressively weaker toward the north. The effect of temperature shifts changed from weakly positive in northern sites to strongly negative in southern ones. The growth trend assessments revealed a significant reduction over the last decades at the southern sites, whereas in the central and northern parts of the network, P. strobus basal area increment shows no significant trends. Across the latitudinal gradient, P. strobus exhibits reduced resistance and recovery in the Southern cluster, whereas overall resilience does not differ significantly. These findings demonstrate that P. strobus possesses considerable climatic plasticity but also increasing sensitivity to high temperatures, particularly at the southern margin of the study network. Consequently, progressive warming and the increasing frequency of waves and droughts will reduce growth potential in southern Europe. Despite generally favorable habitat indicators at the northern sites, temporal trends indicate increasingly negative correlations with summer temperatures, indicating increasing heat sensitivity even there.

title: Assessing maize yield losses from stage-specific agro-meteorological stresses in China’s semi-humid and humid regions
Quantifying the understory light environment of shade-grown coffee with handheld SLAM-LiDAR: A proof-of-concept in three agroforestry systems
Soil moisture dominates the environmental response of tree radial growth at global scales
abstract: Tree radial growth is influenced by multiple environmental factors, but comprehensive global-scale assessments remain scarce. Here, we integrated multiple core environmental variables affecting tree growth and used an integrated response index to quantify tree responses to individual and combined factors, characterize their spatiotemporal patterns, and identify underlying mechanisms. Soil moisture has emerged as the primary driver of tree growth, and deep soil water likely serves as the potential water source for sustaining radial growth in most trees. Trees exhibited contrasting spatial responses: solar radiation (representing light availability), thermal conditions (air and soil temperatures), and wind generally had negative effects, whereas moisture (atmospheric precipitation and soil moisture) and CO₂ promoted growth. North America and Asia showed similar integrated patterns, while Europe differed due to climatic and topographic contrasts. Over time, responses to water-related factors have strengthened, whereas those to other factors have weakened. Increasing dependence on soil moisture across major regions suggests growing constraints from water availability. Soil nutrient status, particularly the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio (C/N), non-linearly modulates the sensitivity of tree growth to soil moisture. We found that a low C/N ratio (threshold < 6.5) is more conducive to expression of moisture-driven growth, confirming that hydro-nutritional synergistic coupling is a core dynamic mechanism driving tree radial growth. Therefore, future forest management should prioritize the dynamic balance of soil C/N stoichiometry alongside the maintenance of water availability.

title: Advancing satellite-driven monitoring of phenological responses to extreme climatic events in the Alpine space
abstract: Climate extremes driven by climate change, such as heatwaves and severe droughts, have significantly impacted the ecosystem of the European Alps. Climate projections indicate that the frequency and intensity of such extreme events in this region will continue to rise. However, it remains unclear how heatwaves and extreme droughts affect the long-term evolution of local vegetation. Long-term time-series of satellite-based vegetation indices and climate records were analyzed to catch effects of climate extremes on spatiotemporal trends of plant phenology. MODIS data from the Alpine space was processed for a 23-year range (2001 to 2023). Correlation between anomalies in the length of the growing season (LOS) and extreme droughts and heatwaves were analyzed. Results indicated that the impact of these climate extremes on plant phenology varies significantly across different phenological stages and regions. Heatwaves led to an earlier onset of SOS primarily in the western high-altitude areas (-0.23 to -0.41 days yr⁻¹), whereas in the lower eastern mountainous regions, they resulted in a later onset of SOS. The consistency analysis between climate extremes and LOS showed that negative LOS anomalies were primarily caused by extreme droughts, which account for 65.4% of cases. Additionally, in drought-dominated areas, approximately 78% of the LOS shortening can be attributed to earlier EOS. Regions under extreme drought stress were mainly located in the southwestern and eastern low-altitude areas of the Alpine space. Furthermore, compound drought-heatwave events significantly shorten LOS across different areas (coincidence rate = 0.68). The study highlighted how remote sensing can advance understanding of mixed effects of extreme droughts and heatwaves on plant phenology considering also the spatial context.

title: Agrivoltaic systems can improve agricultural yield by mitigating extreme plant temperatures
abstract: Agriculture suffers from more intense, prolonged, and frequent extreme temperature events such as heat waves, droughts, and frosts. Agrivoltaic systems offer an opportunity to mitigate such events by deploying photovoltaic (PV) panels above crops. In this study, measurements of plant, air, and soil temperatures, along with solar and infrared radiation, wind speed, and soil moisture demonstrate that plants benefit from cooler microclimates beneath PV panels during extreme heat events, and conversely from warmer microclimates during cold nights. More precisely, during the 2025 heat wave in France, plant temperatures beneath PV panels were observed to be up to 12 °C lower than the 45 °C recorded ones in a control zone without PV panels. Additionally, during radiation-driven spring nights, PV panels helped maintain positive plant surface temperatures. In contrast, plant surface temperatures dropped to -3 °C in the control zone, reaching the threshold at which irreversible crop damage typically begins. Quantifying the impact of PV panels on agricultural yield requires a multi-scale temporal analysis that captures their instantaneous effects on the microclimate, the occurrence of sub-daily extreme events, and their influence on crop growth throughout the season. To this end, the Farquhar photosynthesis model, using the experimental data as inputs, and the STICS crop growth model were both evaluated under stressed and non-stressed conditions. The results suggest that when extreme temperatures occur the PV-induced loss in solar radiation can be turned into a gain in agricultural yield.

title: A deep geostatistical fusion framework for forest canopy height retrieval in complex tropical terrain
Strong canopy wind gusts across a topographic gradient and associated rainfall conditions in a Central Amazon forest
authors: Gabriel Henrique Pires de Mello Ribeiro
abstract: Wind disturbances shape forest structure and dynamics, yet direct observations of strong canopy wind gusts remain scarce. We developed a method to detect and characterize strong canopy wind gusts using 24 months (October 2021–September 2023) of high-frequency (1 Hz) meteorological measurements from an old-growth Central Amazon forest. Strong canopy wind gusts were defined as events with speed ≥10 m s⁻¹, representing the upper tail of the wind speed distribution and approaching speeds associated with tree snapping and uprooting in our study region. We identified 424 events, with maximum speeds reaching 17.9 m s⁻¹ and durations up to 90 s. Events occurred on ∼18% of observation days (∼4% of total observation time), with 3.1 ± 2.9 (mean ± standard deviation) events day⁻¹ and 17.2 ± 9.6 month⁻¹. Wind gusts were more frequent during daytime, although their intensity did not differ between day and night. Differences across the topographic gradient emerged at higher wind speeds, with the strongest and longest-lasting events occurring more frequently on elevated plateau. Gusts occurred year-round but were most frequent during the dry-to-wet transition (September–October). Significant relationships between rainfall intensity and gust frequency and duration emerged only during the most intense rainfall events, particularly above the 87th percentile (∼40 mm h⁻¹). However, gusts commonly preceded heavy rainfall by 5–20 min, consistent with convective outflow processes and indicating spatial and temporal decoupling between wind and rainfall. These findings provide high-resolution, site-level insights into canopy wind variability and its links to local atmospheric and environmental conditions in tropical forests.

title: Evaluating OpenET evapotranspiration estimates in California vineyards: Insights from the GRAPEX experiment
abstract: California agriculture faces escalating water-management challenges from drought and heat while adapting to groundwater-sustainability policies. Accurate field-scale evapotranspiration (ET) values are essential for irrigation decisions and water conservation. OpenET integrates six satellite-based ET models in Google Earth Engine to provide near–real-time actual ET (ET a ) at 30 m and daily resolution. We evaluated OpenET against eddy-covariance ET a from 11 wine-grape vineyards monitored by the Grape Remote sensing Atmospheric Profile & Evapotranspiration eXperiment (GRAPEX). We compared individual-model and ensemble ET a to tower ET a and conducted site-focused analyses to diagnose performance under key microclimate and management conditions. The OpenET ensemble ET a value closely matched tower ET a (daily R 2 = 0.82; MAE = 0.63 mm d -1 ; monthly R 2 = 0.89; MAE = 14.8 mm month -1 ) with negligible bias and generally outperformed individual models. Performance improved with temporal aggregation, consistent with reduced sensitivity to Landsat overpass timing and reference ET-based interpolation at the daily timestep. Skill was highest at monthly and seasonal scales, while daily errors increased during advective conditions and short-lived irrigation deficits, and tower energy-balance closure influenced inferred bias at advection-prone sites. Controlled experiments showed that thermal-based models detected imposed vine water-stress responses directionally (but were dampened in the ensemble) and that winter cover crops, and vine-row orientation produced consistent ET a shifts that propagated into thermal-based OpenET values. These results quantify when OpenET is most reliable for precision viticulture and provide guidance for using satellite ET a to support irrigation scheduling and water accounting in practice.

title: Carbon acquisition and transpiration water consumption strategies of trees in different canopy layers of a cold-temperate Betula platyphylla secondary forest
Diurnally asymmetric impacts of heatwaves on vegetation net primary production across China
Flexible water uptake across soil depths buffers transpiration in winter cereals during dry spells
abstract: Croplands are among the land systems most vulnerable to shifts in precipitation regimes and prolonged droughts, particularly in temperate climates. Characterizing root water uptake patterns is therefore essential to understand how crops maintain function and sustain transpiration under drought stress. We investigated water uptake patterns of winter cereals (wheat, barley) across two contrasting growing seasons (2024, 2025) at a temperate cropland in Central Germany. Within the footprint of an eddy covariance (EC) tower, we sampled plant leaves, precipitation, soil water, and groundwater for stable water isotope analysis at natural abundance and estimated xylem water isotope composition using the Craig–Gordon model. Soil moisture was monitored at nine depths (5–100 cm) at three profiles. Using multi-layer soil moisture time series and a dual-isotope mixing model, we identified the contribution of different water sources to transpiration, and quantified water uptake depth patterns.In 2024, more frequent rainfall maintained wetter soil layers and higher evapotranspiration (ET), whereas 2025 was marked by longer dry spells and consistently lower ET, although average water-use efficiency remained similar with greater variability in 2025. Both crop types exhibited flexibility in water uptake depth in response to dry spells, including access to deeper soil layers (> 60 cm). However, the median uptake depth ranged from 20–60 cm for wheat in 2024, whereas barley met transpiration demand primarily from 10–40 cm despite drier conditions in 2025. Our findings suggest that water uptake strategies are tightly linked to plant traits, access to deeper water sources, and dry spell characteristics, which together shape root plasticity and modulate the impact of drought on transpiration and ecosystem productivity.

title: Contrasting climatic controls on bimodal growth of Pinus elliottii plantations between northern and southern subtropical zones
Editorial Board
Vegetation photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration model: Improved estimation of diurnal, seasonal and interannual dynamics of carbon fluxes at eddy covariance tower sites
Local forest structure modifies realized climate vulnerability under macroclimatic forcing: Attribution from a national forest inventory
Rethinking isotopic evapotranspiration partitioning in extreme drylands: A multi-field coupled framework
Climate-driven expansion and richness hotspots of forest insect pests revealed by stacked species distribution models
A process-based spring phenology framework for projecting climate-change constraints on Chinese hickory cultivation areas
Strengthened sink control under heatwaves contributes to changes in the phenological sequence of photosynthesis and growth
abstract: Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, with profound consequences for forest carbon cycling. Photosynthesis (source) and radial stem growth (sink) are two key processes underpinning this carbon cycle, yet their coordination under heat stress remains unclear. We quantified heatwave-induced changes in source-sink dynamics at 19 European forest sites during the record-breaking heatwaves of 2015 and 2018. We combined FLUXNET-derived gross primary production (GPP, representing photosynthesis) with high-resolution dendrometer data (radial stem growth), and applied the convergent cross-mapping (CCM) method to quantify the causal relationships between photosynthesis and radial stem growth under heatwaves. Our results showed that in evergreen needleleaf forests (ENF), GPP typically peaks before radial growth (4.7 days), but heatwaves reversed this phenological sequence, with growth peaking earlier than photosynthesis (–10.0 days). The CCM analysis further showing that bidirectional source-sink causal effects were strengthened during heatwaves, with the sink-to-source causal effect increasing more in ENF. This heatwave-induced phenological shift was driven primarily by plant functional type (21.4%), with additional contributions from increased summer temperature (11.4%) and enhanced sink-to-source feedback (9.4%). Overall, our study demonstrates that tree carbon allocation strategies are plastic under extreme climate events and that plant functional types differ fundamentally in the source-sink regulatory responses, with important implications for predicting forest resilience to future climate change.

title: Diagnosing and correcting OpenET satellite evapotranspiration across U.S. climate zones: Error decomposition, explainable AI, and uncertainty quantification
abstract: Satellite evapotranspiration (ET) from the OpenET platform supports water resource management across the United States but exhibits biases that vary by climate. While machine learning (ML) can improve satellite ET accuracy, prior studies report aggregate metrics without explaining how corrections work or providing operational uncertainty quantification. This study applies an XGBoost correction framework integrating OpenET satellite outputs with ground meteorological observations from 22 AmeriFlux cropland eddy covariance sites across six Köppen climate zones. The framework achieved 41.9% RMSE improvement over OpenET, while a configuration excluding all ground meteorological inputs still achieved 28.5% improvement. Error decomposition revealed that the dominant correction mechanism shifts seasonally: summer corrections were driven primarily by bias removal (61.3% of improvement), reflecting systematic overestimation during peak ET, while winter corrections were driven by variance reduction (96.8%), addressing satellite noise from cloud contamination. Across climates, humid zones improved primarily through variance reduction (68–81%), while water limited zones, including BSk and dry-summer Csa sites, benefited more from bias correction (40–52%). SHAP analysis stratified by climate yielded patterns consistent with these mechanisms. Leave-one-site-out cross-validation indicated strong transferability in humid climates (Dwb R² = 0.82) but limited generalization in BSk sites (R² = −0.30), while leave-one-cluster-out validation provided a more conservative spatial-transferability estimate by accounting for colocated site clusters. Conformal prediction provided empirical uncertainty quantification: constant-width intervals achieved 92.6% overall coverage, while climate-adaptive intervals produced environment specific uncertainty bounds ranging from ±0.81 to ±2.13 mm/day across climates. This framework provides a pathway toward operational ET correction with uncertainty bounds and diagnostic insights for satellite algorithm improvement.

title: High-resolution actual evapotranspiration in almond orchards by integrating physiological and TSEB models
abstract: Spatial and temporal high-resolution thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing systems are emerging as valuable tools for monitoring crop water use and stress. Thermal cameras onboard small uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) provide high spatial and temporal resolution TIR. Reliable high-resolution TIR imagery is a crucial input for remote sensing-based land surface energy balance models in mapping instantaneous actual evapotranspiration (ET a ). Therefore, evaluating UAS-acquired TIR temperature correction and ET a upscaling method is needed to improve the accuracy of instantaneous and daily ET a , respectively. In this study, we applied a novel physiological-surface energy balance-based TIR temperature correction, a key input for the two-source energy balance (TSEB) model, in combination with a daily ET a upscaling method, to estimate high-resolution ET a at almond orchards in California. A coupled physiological model was developed and compared to in-situ physiological measurements of net CO 2 assimilation rate (A n ), stomatal conductance (g s ), and leaf temperature (T l ). The TSEB Priestley-Taylor (TSEB-PT) and contextual approach (TSEB-2T) models were applied to UAS imagery and proximal tower data, and their performance was compared with eddy covariance (EC) measurements. For ET a to be useful for irrigation scheduling, upscaling methods based on solar radiation (R s ) and TSEB time series of hourly modeled LE (latent heat flux) were evaluated using EC measurements. Results showed that the coupled physiological and surface energy balance model predicted T l in good agreement with observed canopy temperature (T c ), with the highest R 2 (0.92–0.98) and the lowest RMSE (0.84–1.6 °C). Applying physiological-surface energy balance-based TIR temperature correction to UAS-acquired TIR imagery improved LE estimates, reducing the MAE by 18.3%. The upscaling methods performed best when using instantaneous LE values between 11:00 and 13:00, with RMSE from 0.02 to 0.65 mm day −1 based on EC measurements. The TSEB-2T UAS-CMT and R s upscaling method outperformed the other scenarios, with RMSE of 0.66 mm day −1 . This study demonstrates the potential to enhance the accuracy of high-spatial-resolution ET a estimates in cropping systems, supporting precision irrigation.

title: Nocturnal long-range transport of Alternaria spores in Central Europe: synoptic and boundary-layer drivers
Observation-constrained assessment of long-term cropland productivity trends and drivers at the global scale
abstract: The cropland ecosystem is closely linked to global food security and carbon budget dynamics. Understanding the trends and drivers of cropland gross primary productivity (GPP) is essential for evaluating potential agricultural yields and for formulating effective adaptation and even mitigation strategies. However, existing GPP assessments have largely focused on natural ecosystems, with limited attention paid to the long-term evolution of cropland productivity and its attribution. Our study presents a global analysis of cropland GPP from 1982 to 2016, with an attribution analysis constrained by multi-source observational datasets. Findings reveal a notable increase in cropland GPP, averaging 10.4 Pg C yr −1 , which accounts for 8.6% of global GPP and contributes 18.8% to its overall rise, only followed by evergreen broadleaf forests. Since 2000, croplands have emerged as the largest contributor to global GPP gains (22.5%). Attribution analysis indicates that vegetation structural changes explain approximately 43% of the cropland GPP increase, while climate variability imposes a negative −9% effect. The remaining increase is dominated by residual term that combines rising atmospheric CO 2 , intensified management, crop breeding and differences among GPP products. By further quantifying the plant-assisted weathering efficiency (PAWE), we show that the biological enhancement of weathering rises nonlinearly with productivity, yielding a 2.5–4.5-fold biological amplification across major breadbaskets. Realized carbon removal nonetheless remains contingent on mineral supply, soil chemistry, hydrology, and alkalinity export.

title: Moso bamboo expansion impacts on root respiration of Japanese cedar forest and secondary broad-leaved forest in a socio-ecological production landscape
abstract: Soil respiration and its root-derived component are important pathways for carbon release from forest ecosystems, but they remain poorly understood in expanding bamboo forests. We quantified root respiration and its drivers in an abandoned Moso bamboo forest (BF), a Japanese cedar forest (CF), and a mixed evergreen and deciduous broad-leaved forest (DF) in southwestern Japan during eight campaigns from April 2024 to March 2025. Using soil coring, we measured respiration from extracted living roots ( R a ) together with fine- and coarse-root biomass. Nonlinear mixed-effects models describing R a responses to soil temperature ( T s ) and soil moisture ( θ ) were constructed. Mean R a was highest in BF (0.285 g CO 2 m −2 h −1 ), followed by DF (0.255 g CO 2 m −2 h −1 ) and CF (0.057 g CO 2 m −2 h −1 ). Fine-root temperature sensitivity and mass-specific respiration were lower in BF, indicating that physiological activity alone did not explain the elevated R a . Instead, R a was strongly influenced by fine-root biomass, which was approximately three times greater in BF than in DF and fifteen times greater than in CF. As a result, biomass-driven enhancement increased R a in BF relative to CF, whereas lower mass-specific respiration in BF offset its biomass advantage over DF. Shapley-based contribution analysis supported these interpretations by revealing that fine-root biomass was the dominant positive driver of differences in R a , whereas physiological factors partly offset the biomass effect. These local comparisons highlight that root respiration is shaped by combined biomass and physiological effects, whose relative importance differs among adjacent forest stands.

title: Multi-variable evaluation of agroecosystem models reveals challenges in daily and annual NEE simulation for croplands
abstract: Net ecosystem exchange (NEE) of CO₂ is the residual of two opposing fluxes, and accuracy at the modelled NEE level can eclipse compensating errors in its components. This study evaluated DNDCv.CAN and EPIC against multi-variable observations at two Manitoba agricultural sites across 17 site-years. The two sites were Carberry (CAB, synthetic fertilizers, irrigated) and South Tobacco Creek (STC, manure-amended, rainfed). NEE was used as a diagnostic indicator of model structure. Component decomposition into gross primary production (GPP) and ecosystem respiration (R eco ), compensating-error analysis, and conditional residual binning were applied. Both models reproduced soil temperature, evapotranspiration, and yield with low error. Daily growing-season NEE from DNDCv.CAN had R² = 0.68 at CAB and R² = 0.33 at STC. EPIC returned R² = 0.49 at CAB and 0.29 at STC. DNDCv.CAN systematically under-predicted both GPP and R eco by similar magnitudes and the same sign at both sites. Roughly 10 to 28 % of growing-season days showed component error cancellation in NEE. R eco showed negative Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency at the daily scale and systematic under-prediction at the annual scale. STC was a net carbon source in 2014, 2015, and 2016, but both models predicted a net sink in all three years. Soybean at STC showed the weakest agreement with observations across all twelve site-crop component evaluations. Structural improvements are needed in respiration partitioning in DNDCv.CAN, in soybean representation under manure-amended soils, and in interannual soil water carryover in EPIC. Daily-scale multi-variable validation with component decomposition provides a diagnostic framework for identifying structural limitations that net-flux metrics obscure.

title: Time-lagged ozone and environmental controls on overstorey–understorey water-use dynamics in a Mediterranean forest revealed by empirical dynamic modeling
abstract: Tropospheric ozone (O 3 ) affects plant physiological processes, yet its role in regulating water-use dynamics across vertical forest layers remains poorly understood. Because stomatal regulation and whole-tree hydraulic processes operate over different temporal scales, accounting for time-lagged responses is essential for understanding stand-level water use. This study investigated how O 3 , vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and soil water content (SWC) influence tree water use and its vertical coupling in a Mediterranean forest. Two-year sap flow ( S f ) measurements from overstorey Quercus ilex and understorey layer Phillyrea latifolia trees were analyzed using empirical dynamic modeling (EDM), combining unified information-theoretic causality and S-map analyses. VPD exerted relatively short-term causal influences on tree water use, particularly stomatal conductance ( g t ), whereas SWC effects generally extended over lags of 0–4 days and varied with soil depth, ecosystem layer, and year. O 3 showed delayed causal influences on S f , with peak lags of approximately 2 days in overstorey and 4 days in understorey trees, with temporal variation in the estimated lags (0–5 and 1–4 days, respectively). O 3 effects on g t occurred at shorter time scales and differed between ecosystem layers and years: in the cooler and wetter summer of 2014, O 3 had a negative effect on overstorey g t , but a positive effect on understorey g t , whereas the overstorey effect shifted to positive in the hotter and drier summer of 2015. A significant causal influence of understorey S f on overstorey S f , but not in the reverse direction, was detected, suggesting that this interaction may arise from differences in water acquisition together with shared environmental forcing. These findings show that forest water use emerges from nonlinear and time-lagged responses to interacting atmospheric and soil drivers, highlighting the importance of considering O 3 effects together with drought stress when predicting Mediterranean forest responses to environmental change.

title: Assessing silvicultural treatment effects on catchment hydrology under current and future climate scenarios
abstract: Water scarcity is an increasingly pressing issue in Mediterranean mountains, where interannual variability in precipitation, global warming, and widespread forest regrowth after land abandonment have reduced streamflow. In this context, forest management, particularly silvicultural thinning, is crucial for mitigating the impacts of Global Change in Mediterranean forests. This study assesses the sensitivity of ecohydrological responses (Leaf Area Index (LAI), Evapotranspiration (ET), and mean and maximum streamflow) to two contrasting thinning strategies (Uniform Shelterwood System (USS) and Group Selection System (GSS)) under three climate scenarios (SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP5–8.5). The analysis was conducted in the San Salvador catchment, a representative Mediterranean mountain catchment in the Central Pyrenees, dominated by Pinus sylvestris . Field observations were used to calibrate and validate the Regional Hydro-Ecologic Simulation System (RHESSys). Results show that: (i) both thinning strategies significantly reduced LAI, whereas the effects on ET and streamflow depended on the silvicultural system applied; (ii) USS did not produce statistically significant changes in ET, mean streamflow or peakflow relative to no-management scenario; (iii) GSS significantly reduced ET and increased mean and peak streamflow under the milder scenarios, and the contrast between both systems indicates that the spatial configuration, and not only its intensity, conditions the catchment-scale response; (iv) under the most extreme scenario (SSP5–8.5), thinning effects on ET and streamflow were attenuated or negligible under both USS and GSS strategies, highlighting the limits of management under intensified climatic stressors; (v) RHESSys provides a robust framework for evaluating coupled vegetation-hydrology dynamics under silvicultural interventions in data-scarce Mediterranean mountains. Anticipating the hydrological impacts of thinning constitutes a key challenge for forest managers. Integrating hydrologically oriented practices into adaptive landscape planning could improve water provisioning services to downstream areas and strengthen the resilience of Mediterranean mountain landscapes under future climate trajectories.

title: Decreased precipitation frequency increases nitrogen loss across degraded grasslands in a two-year mesocosm experiment
Flash drought promotes decoupling of soil CO2 emissions and CH4 uptake in seasonal subtropical wetlands: A case study in Dongting Lake
Adapting Noah-MP-Crop for sorghum modeling in a semi-arid environment: a case study of Gedaref region in East Sahel
abstract: Semi-arid agricultural regions are highly vulnerable to rainfall variability and heat stress, yet crop modeling in these areas is often constrained by limited field observations. Land surface models provide an important advantage over standalone crop models by simulating crop growth within a coupled water-energy-carbon framework, enabling interactions between vegetation development and land-atmosphere exchanges. This study adapted the Noah-MP-Crop model to simulate rainfed sorghum in Sudan’s Gedaref region by introducing sorghum-specific phenological and physiological parameters. To represent spatial and interannual variability in sowing timing, we used normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) data from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) to estimate sowing dates. The model was calibrated using a stepwise approach constrained by satellite-derived leaf area index (LAI), observation-based surface energy fluxes, and multi-year field yield observations. The adapted model reproduced the seasonal evolution of sorghum canopy development and surface energy fluxes across different hydro-climatic conditions. Compared with a conventional fixed sowing-date approach, dynamic sowing improved LAI simulation during validation, increasing Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) from 0.27 to 0.57 while reducing mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.21 to 0.16. Dynamic sowing also improved yield simulation, reducing MAE by 27% during calibration and 55% during validation relative to the fixed sowing date approach. The results indicate that integrating satellite-derived sowing dates with crop-specific calibration improves sorghum growth simulation in the rainfed Gedaref region.

title: Corrigendum to “The microclimate in post-wildfire areas in northern New Mexico: modeling plant stress” [Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, 2026(389) 111399]
Moderate thinning enhances drought resistance of Chinese cork oak plantation
Weather adjusted next-season pollen integrals improve airborne birch pollen forecasts
Drought tolerance and mortality risk of European beech
abstract: Little is known about the drought-induced mortality risk for most tree species. This makes it difficult to predict their future distribution. Here, we quantified the drought tolerance and mortality risk of the economically important European beech ( Fagus sylvatica L.) by analysing its response to decreasing water potentials in the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. From 2014 to 2023, we measured ecohydrological parameters at eight forest sites covering a large part of the species' ecological niche. The hourly time series at all sites included temperature, vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and soil water potential (Ψ soil ). At one site, the time series also included soil hydraulic conductivity (K), root water uptake (RWU), changes in stem radius, and dendrometer-derived leaf water potential (Ψ leaf ). Additionally, we determined the annual mortality rate of beech trees at all sites. At sites with a positive climatic water balance, beech mortality only occurred in soils with a low water storage capacity. However, at sites with a negative climatic water balance, beech trees also died in soils with high storage capacities. Mortality dynamics indicated that Ψ soil was more important for beech decline than VPD, heat, and excessive radiation. An average Ψ soil of −0.8 MPa in the root zone was identified as the mortality threshold for all sites, as beyond this threshold, RWU ceased due to extremely low K. Consequently, tree water reserves were largely depleted, and the percent loss of xylem conductivity exceeded 50% induced by midday Ψ leaf values as low as −3.5 MPa. Beyond the mortality threshold, annual mortality rates increased with the duration of drought. Furthermore, our study shows that the recent increase in beech mortality is induced by increased atmospheric drought, earlier leaf sprouting, and incomplete soil water replenishment during winter. These factors have resulted in more frequent soil drying and threshold exceedances in recent years.

title: Corrigendum to “A dynamic OPTRAM soil moisture constraint for PT-JPL evapotranspiration from Sentinel-2 validated across land covers and climates” [Agricultural and Forest Meteorology 388 (2026) 111375]
Why sensible and latent heat fluxes vary differently with height: horizontal advection and multiscale turbulent transport over a heterogeneous surface
abstract: Eddy-covariance fluxes measured over heterogeneous surfaces may not represent lower-level exchange when sensible heat (SH) and latent heat (LE) vary with height in the atmospheric surface layer. This problem is especially relevant over irrigated land adjacent to warmer, drier terrain, where horizontal advection can modify turbulent transport. Using two-level EC measurements over an irrigated cotton field, we examine why SH and LE differ between 8.7 m and 2.7 m during daytime. Four recurring SH–LE convergence/divergence classes were identified and analyzed using complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) and complementary turbulence diagnostics. Middle- and large-scale motions distinguished the classes, whereas small-scale turbulence provided mainly a background contribution. The clearest mechanism was reduced vertical mixing aloft: vertical-velocity variance and transport efficiency weakened more at 8.7 m, especially at middle scales. Altered downward scalar transport provided a secondary, more interpretive explanation for the contrasting SH and LE responses. Late-afternoon negative SH and stable near-surface conditions were consistent with oasis-effect behavior in this advection-favorable setting. Together, the results show that recurring SH–LE flux-gradient states reflect systematic differences in multiscale, height-dependent transport and caution against assuming that a single-height EC flux represents exchange below the measurement level.

title: Effects of forest structure, tree species, and weather conditions on the intra-annual variability of air temperature buffering in temperate forests
abstract: Air temperature buffering effects by forest canopies have important consequences for ecosystem functioning. Yet, knowledge about the relationship between forest structure and the intra-annual variability of air temperature buffering remains scarce. Here, we investigated the intra-annual variability of air temperature buffering by forest canopies using a paired design of weather stations in permanent forest plots (n = 134) of pure European beech, Norway spruce, and Scots pine as well as neighboring open lands (n = 48) on three sites in Central Europe. We found that air temperature buffering follows a seasonal pattern, with buffering effects being strongest during summer and weakest, or even absent, during winter. We then used terrestrial laser scanning (TLS)-derived measures of canopy openness and vertical structure to test whether the intra-annual variability of air temperature buffering is driven by forest structure and how these effects covary with weather conditions and landscape factors. For coniferous stands, forest structure explained on average 10.7% of variance in air temperature buffering throughout the year. For broadleaved stands, forest structure explained on average only 2.4% of variance in air temperature buffering during winter and 4.8% in summer. Overall, the most explained variance was attributable to weather conditions (Ø 40.8%) and landscape factors (Ø 13.0%), while forest structure explained only 8.3% on average. Our results suggest that the influence of forest management on air temperature buffering is limited within the studied forest types, highlighting a limited potential to mitigate the effects of climate change-related weather extremes on forest microclimate through adapted forest management and structures.

title: Quantifying between and within tree stem variations using dendrometers
abstract: Dendrometers have been widely studied for irrigation management in apple orchards, yet the high variability of dendrometer-derived parameters among trees remains a challenge for reliable irrigation control. This study quantify the variability of key dendrometer parameters commonly proposed for irrigation management usage between and within trees. In addition, continuous microtensiometer measurements of trunk water potential (Ψtrunk) and standard stem water potential measurements using a Scholander pressure chamber (Ψstem) were compared with dendrometer-derived growth and tree water deficit (TWD). The number of sensors required to achieve a 0.15 MPa (Ψtrunk) standard error was then calculated. All tree water status proxies showed higher variability than Ψstem. Dendrometer parameters showed greater variability within trees than between trees, indicating substantial heterogeneity across stem positions. When using TWDmax as Ѱtrunk predictor, nine sensors were required to achieve 0.15 MPa standard error (coefficient of variation = 0.123). Tolerating a bigger variability of 0.2 MPa, 5 dendrometers need to be used. Daily Ψtrunk minimum and TWDmax were well correlated (R2m and R²c = 0.73), although this correlation was weaker and tree dependent for Ψtrunk maximum and TWDmin (R2m = 0.06, R²c = 0.32). This reflects their shared measurement location conditions and supports the suitability of dendrometers for monitoring tree water status, especially in the middle of the day. Options to reduce the observed variability in dendrometers, especially during the night, should be studied.

title: Differences in the climate sensitivity of tree growth and latewood blue intensity across contiguous and disjunct populations of Tsuga canadensis in the eastern United States
Climate-adaptive optimization of rice sowing windows for yield stability: A case study of Anhui, China
Towards realistic representation of forest management and stand age dynamics in a terrestrial biosphere model (DLEM): impacts on forest carbon dynamics in the Southeastern United States
